## Problem

Slack is a workplace messaging platform that enables users to exchange direct messages and create topic-based group channels. Users can share text and media, with notifications delivered in real time across multiple devices.

We are designing the core messaging layer: direct messages between two users and group channels whose membership can range from a few people to tens of thousands. The central challenge is that small conversations benefit from eager push delivery for a real-time feel, while per-message push in massive channels is prohibitively expensive and requires a fundamentally different approach.

### Functional requirements

- Users can send direct messages (DMs) to another individual user.
- Users can create a group channel and manage its membership (add or remove members).
- Users can send text messages with optional image attachments to a channel; the message is delivered to all members.
- Online users receive new messages in real time through persistent connections.
- Users can delete their own messages (a soft delete that other participants can see).

**Out of scope (below the line)**

- Threaded replies and message threading
- Message reactions, emoji, and editing
- Voice and video calls
- File sharing beyond images
- Channel discovery and public channels
- End-to-end encryption
- Typing indicators and presence
- Mobile push notification pipeline (APNs / Firebase Cloud Messaging)
- Multi-region deployment

### Non-functional requirements

- Messages reach online recipients within `200ms` for DMs and small channels, and within `500ms` for large channels.
- Target `99.9%` uptime for the message send path. Sends always succeed even if some delivery paths degrade.
- Once the server accepts a message, it must never be lost. Persist before acknowledging the send.
- Support `50M` daily active users, approximately `1B` messages per day, with channels ranging from 2 members (DM) to `100K+` members.
- Messages within a single channel appear in consistent order across all clients.
- Users logged in on multiple devices receive messages on all active sessions.

### Assumptions

- A DM is modeled internally as a two-member channel.
- Channel membership is invite-only. No public channel discovery.
- Rich media means image uploads only. Videos and files are out of scope.
- Deletion is soft: the message body is replaced with a "deleted" marker.
- Single-region deployment for this design.
- User authentication and profiles are assumed to exist.

### Back-of-the-envelope estimation

| Metric | Value | Drives |
|---|---|---|
| Daily active users (DAU) | `50M` | Sizes the WebSocket connection fleet |
| Messages per day | `~1B` | Confirms write-heavy workload needs Cassandra-class throughput |
| Messages per second (avg) | `~12K` | Sizes the message service and storage write path |
| Peak messages per second | `~50K` (burst) | Confirms need for horizontal scaling on the write path |
| Concurrent WebSocket connections | `~10M` (20% of DAU online) | Sizes the WebSocket gateway fleet |
| Average message size | `~500 bytes` text + metadata | Storage: `~500 GB/day` raw messages |
| Channel size range | 2 (DM) to `100K+` | Defines the push vs. pull delivery threshold |

The connection count confirms that a single server cannot hold all WebSocket connections. A fleet of gateway servers is required, with a routing layer to deliver messages to the correct server. The message volume confirms that the storage layer must handle sustained high write throughput, making Cassandra a natural fit for the message log. The channel size range is the most consequential number: delivering to a 5-person DM is fundamentally different from delivering to a 100K-member announcement channel, and the architecture must handle both.

## Hints

<details>
<summary>Hint 1</summary>

Use a publish-subscribe model (e.g., Redis Pub/Sub) to broadcast new messages to all 500 participants in real time.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2</summary>

Store the most recent 30–40 messages in a Redis sorted set or list with an LRU eviction policy to keep memory bounded.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3</summary>

For low-latency retrieval, cache the recent messages in memory on each client or use a dedicated cache layer.

</details>
